utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First, I would like to be sure that the interpretation booths are working properly, and that everybody hears when I speak. Turning first to my colleagues, the Judges, do you hear properly? Then the Registrar? Office of the Prosecutor? All right. The hearing has been opened. Turning to the Registrar, would you please call the cases before us today?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-5-R61, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, and case IT-95-18-R61, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First, I would like to know who is representing the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg, one of the senior trial attorneys of this Tribunal; I appear at this hearing with my learned friends, Mr. Mark Harmon and Mr. Terree Bowers. We are assisted as legal advisers by Payam Akhavan and to operate the technical equipment we bring the researcher, Todd Cleaver. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostberg. We are now meeting as part of Rule 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Rule provides for a proceedings in case there is a failure to execute a warrant of arrest. Therefore, this is an ex parte proceeding and I want to say outside of the presence of the parties since the parties were served with the indictment and the warrants of arrest which were relative to the case. This hearing today deals were two indictments; an indictment dealing with the general policy carried out in Bosnia and Herzegovina by the accused Mr. Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. The first indictment was confirmed by Judge Jorda in July 1995. The second indictment, which is the subject of this hearing, that is, the failure to execute a warrant of arrest, deals with the events which took place in Srebrenica in July 1995. The second indictment was confirmed along with the subsequent warrants of arrest in November 1995. In addition, the Registrar of the Tribunal was seized yesterday afternoon by an act from Mr. Radovan Karadzic asking that Igor Pantelic represent the defendant. Could you tell what the Trial Chamber's decision about this request was? Turning to the Registrar, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The Registrar of the Tribunal hereby confirms that yesterday afternoon Mr. Pantelic from the Belgrade Bar filed with us an act which I will read asking for Power of Attorney. "I authorise Igor Pantelic, an attorney from Belgrade, residing at 20 Vojvode Dobrnjast Street to represent me before the International Tribunal in The Hague, and to take any legal measures that would be in my interest. The above mentioned person", that is Mr. Pantelic, "may later on establish a team of lawyers who will work in my interest and with my prior consent". Signed Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Pale, 25 June 1996. Following the filing of this act, we immediately contacted the Trial Chamber which took a decision yesterday evening which I will report on now. The Trial Chamber I composed of Mr. Claude Jorda presiding, Mrs. Elizabeth Odio Benito, Mr. Fouad Riad, assisted by Mr. Dominique Marro, Deputy Registrar, decision of 26th June 1996, the Prosecutor against Radovan Karadzic, requests additional information. The Trial Chamber, given Articles 21 of the Statute and 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, seized by the Prosecutor for the purposes of a new review of the indictments against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic in case IT-95-5-R61, IT-95-18-R61, about which a public hearing shall be held on 26th June 1996 at the seat of the Tribunal in accordance with Rule 61 of the Rules, seized by the Registrar of a request from Radovan Karadzic which was given to his attorney, Mr. Pantelic from Belgrade, is a request for an intervention by this attorney during the hearings for a further review of the indictments. Considering that this act which was submitted to the Trial Chamber as well as the requests in it were formulated in imprecise terms, and for that reason Mr. Pantelic should be asked to clarify in writing the purpose and legal basis for his request seeking an intervention before the Trial Chamber, and states that this written application must be filed with the Registrar on 27th June 1996. Signed Claude Jorda, Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber I. In accordance with the instructions from the Trial Chamber, I have informed by telephone, that is late in the evening, Mr. Pantelic that he would have to make a request giving more details about his request. I can now inform both the Trial Chamber and the Office of the Prosecutor that we have received several months before this hearing begun the text of that new request.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marro. As I have just said, the proceedings under Rule 61 permit proceedings which exclude any agent or proxies, because this is intended for the presentation by the Prosecution of all of the charges against an accused person who, in addition, was informed of the indictments and the warrants of arrest against him. I would like to remind you, so that things be very clear, that these proceedings under Rule 61 are organised when there has been failure to execute the warrant of arrest under reasonable delay and reasonable time periods, that the confirming Judge informs the Prosecutor that he must explain all measures that were taken in order to be sure that the indictments were, in fact, served on the accused and that the arrest warrants were brought to his knowledge. This is an obligatory formality. These were, in fact, carried out by the two confirming Judges, that is, Judge Fouad Riad and Judge Claude Jorda, on 18th June last. The proceedings, therefore, does not allow for the presence of a proxy. Nonetheless, the presence made at the request which has not been very much clarified from Mr. Pantelic makes it necessary for the Tribunal to deliberate immediately in order to come to a decision for the time being and only at this point of the proceedings whether Mr. Pantelic may be admitted into the courtroom. It will now immediately at the Bench deliberate on the question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal has decided that it will allow Mr. Pantelic into the courtroom at this stage of the Tribunal, and he will be here during the reading of his explanatory motion which the Tribunal up to this point has still not been informed of because it was filed barely an hour ago with the Registrar. Turning to the Registrar, I will ask you now to usher Mr. Pantelic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marro. Mr. Pantelic, would you please put your head set on? Could the usher help him to put the head set on the right channel? Mr. Pantelic, do you understand when I speak to you or would you prefer to put on the head set? All right. Turning to you, could you first rise and introduce yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour of the Trial Chamber, honourable Justice Ostberg, I am Igor Pantelic, attorney at law from Belgrade. I am acting as Defence counsel of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, on behalf of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, according to my Power of Attorney which I submitted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. You may be seated. The Tribunal was seized yesterday by a request which was not precise, it was a rather general request, in the interests of your client, one of the two accused, that is, Dr. Karadzic. The Tribunal, as it said before the public, and for a long time now, has requested that additional information be brought to your own application. Mr. Pantelic, the Tribunal which has already seen you in the confines of this institution knows that you understand the rules of proceedings here, and that you are aware of how the International Criminal Tribunal operates -- you and your client as well. The Tribunal has decided that when an attorney comes to this international body, whose rules must conform to the highest standards of international law, both for the Prosecution and for the Defence with the purpose of ensuring an impartial and equitable trial, it was, therefore, proper to listen to what you had to say, first to read and to hear your motion, and to ask you whether this motion really does correspond to what you are thinking. We will have it read by the Registrar. We do not hear it yet, and we will then ask you, Mr. Pantelic, and I will ask you, to be very careful about what I am asking you, to make some very concise explanations. Mr. Marro, would you please read the additional motion which was filed by Mr. Pantelic this morning at 9 o'clock addressed to the Office of the Prosecutor and to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Motion of the Defence in the interests of Radovan Karadzic. In accordance with Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the counsel for the Defence is introducing this application and is affirming the following: 1. On 26th June 1995, the Defence has filed with the Registry a copy of the Power of Attorney which was signed by Radovan Karadzic, according to which he authorises Igor Pantelic to represent him as his attorney before the International Criminal Tribunal. 2. In accordance with Rule 44 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the counsel for the Defence which has been chosen by the accused must file his act with the Registrar as quickly as possible at any stage of the proceedings. 3. Pursuant to Article 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal and to the relevant Articles of the United Nation Covenants on Human Rights and on the safeguard of human rights and fundamental freedoms, any accused person enjoys the fundamental human right, that is, the right to defend himself with an attorney which he himself has chosen without any restriction being placed on this. 4. The presence of the attorney in the courtroom during the presentation of the indictment by the Prosecutor is not counted to the spirit of Rule 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and, in addition, the presence demonstrates in significant efforts that have been made in order to guarantee one of the principal rights, human rights of the accused. The Defence, therefore, asks for the possibility of being present in the courtroom throughout the public hearing which was established in this case, as well as free access to any document and relevant case files which the Prosecutor will submit at this stage of proceedings". Signed Igor Pantelic, The Hague, 27th June 1996. This is a motion which we received around 9.30 this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marro. The Tribunal considers that the 61 proceedings have not yet begun, but does want to hear the very rapid explanations of Mr. Pantelic. As I repeat very briefly and then I say that after these explanations, we will ask for brief explanations from the Office of the Prosecutor. I give you the floor, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition to my motion from this morning submitted to the Registry, I would stress that it is not contrary to the Rule 61 procedure before the Tribunal that the presence of Defence counsel during the review of indictment is not allowed. I want to say that the position of the Defence counsel at this stage of the procedure is completely in accordance with the basic human rights of an accused or a suspect. The Tribunal has very, as I can say, general and large approach to the Rules, and I think that there is a manoeuvring area to allow Defence counsel to follow this procedure review of the indictment in accordance with the position of the Prosecutor and without any particular interfering in that procedure which Defence fully respect. That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. I now turn to the Office of the Prosecutor: Have you any comments that you would like to make, brief ones, please, both about the written motion as given to the Registrar and then to the several of the additional explanations that Mr. Pantelic gave? I give the floor to you, Mr. Ostberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. This comes as a bit of a surprise. I have not seen this written motion until more than two or three minutes ago. Nevertheless, I have some comments. The Prosecution welcomes, of course, the fact that Radovan Karadzic seems to have recognised this Tribunal and filed a Power of Attorney for a Defence lawyer with the Registrar. However, today's hearing is an ex parte hearing, as your Honour has already pointed out, under Rule 61, due to the fact that it has not been possible to execute a warrant of arrest. This is not a trial in absentia. I think, your Honour, that the presence of counsel for the Defence without the accused would transform these proceedings with arguments from the Defence lawyer, etc., into some kind of a trial of absentia which is not permitted under our Statute. Indeed, I think this would prejudice the right of the accused to be tried in his presence under International Human Rights law. I also think what Mr. Pantelic says under paragraph (3) in his written motion about the United Nations Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and European Convention of Human Rights has a basic bearing on a trial and not at such a hearing we are having here today. With his comments, your Honour, I just want to stress that I can see no way of the appearance of Mr. Pantelic unless he brings his client. He is perfectly welcome to follow all our proceedings from the gallery. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostberg. We will suspend the hearing so that we may deliberate on the motion which was presented by Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am going to read out the decision taken by the Chamber and I will try to read it out slowly to make it possible for interpreters to follow me under the best possible conditions so as both parties and the public can understand. The Trial Chamber, pursuant to Articles 21 of the Statute and 61 of the Rules of Procedures and Evidence, pursuant to the decision of the Chamber for an application dealing with additional information dated 26th June 1996, having heard the Registrar reading out the application lodged by Mr. Pantelic and the additional explanation provided by the letter, having heard the Prosecutor in the course of the hearing: Considering that the procedure in case of failure to execute an arrest warrant provided for in Article 61 of the Rules makes it possible to have a new review in the course of a public hearing and by the full Bench of an indictment. Considering that Mr. Pantelic asked to have access to documents and case files that the Prosecutor will tender in the course of the Rule 61 proceedings, cannot be admitted if not within a trial, and after initial appearance of the accused physically present, pursuant to Article 66 of the Rules, that the accused will also enjoy at that particular moment all the other rights which are guaranteed to him by the provisions of Article 21 of the Statute. Considering that Rule 61 proceeding cannot be interpreted as a trial. Considering that these proceedings totally guarantee the rights of the accused and that the letter has been notified, the indictments before this proceedings, on the one hand, and that he also enjoys the right to be present accompanied by his counsel before the Tribunal, on the other hand, and that in this case the proceedings would change its nature and becomes an adversarial trial with all the inherent guarantees to an equitable trial. Considering, however, that the presence of Mr. Pantelic and his application to attend the proceedings pursuant to Article 61 in the physical absence of the accused can, therefore, be interpreted in the present case as being based on one of the general principles of the rights of the Defence, interpreted here as being a right for the best possible information of his client as provided for by Article 21, para 4(a) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Considering that the confirming Judges have deemed in their orders dated 18th June 1996 that the conditions relative to the information provided to the accused Radovan Karadzic have been fully met as demonstrated by the Prosecutor. Considering, however, that the Chamber rules that unless counsel otherwise decides this information could usefully be supplemented today by reading out the indictments in the presence of the counsel selected by the accused. Considering, furthermore, that this Chamber with a view to make it possible for the assigned counsel to inform his client of the charges thinks that a status of observer should be granted to him. For the forgoing reasons, the Chamber takes note of the acts lodged by Mr. Pantelic on behalf of Radovan Karadzic, invites the Registrar to read out the two indictments in the presence of Mr. Pantelic in the courtroom against Radovan Karadzic, unless Mr. Pantelic expressively waives this right; rejects the request by Mr. Pantelic when he wants to remain present in the courtroom throughout the Rule 61 proceedings and have free access to documents and case files that the Prosecutor will tender. We state that Mr. Pantelic will be taken to the public gallery of the courtroom where a seat will be reserved to him throughout the hearing as an observer. Having taken this decision, I am now turning to Mr. Pantelic. I hope that this slow reading of the decision was understood by him. So, this Chamber, unless you otherwise decide, suggests that you remain present in the courtroom only during this particular part of the courtroom when the Registrar will read out in full the two indictments concerning your client. Can you agree with that, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So after this we will take a break and we will resume proceedings later on. We will ask for a seat to be especially reserved to Mr. Pantelic during the other days of this hearing as an observer. So, Registrar, please, are you in a position to read out the two indictments in full issued by the Prosecutor and confirmed respectively in July '95 by Judge Jorda and in November of the same year by Judge Riad? Registrar, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We now turn to the second part of this indictment; shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you like to take a sip of water or be replaced? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Part II.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marro, you have just read the first indictment. The Tribunal, once you have had a drink of water, wants you to now read the second indictment which is a part of this 61 hearing. Would you like to rest for a few moments? All right. You can now begin reading the second indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Registrar, the Tribunal would like to thank you in line with the decision that we took that we would have the two indictments read out in full in the presence of Mr. Pantelic in the courtroom. At the present, we are adjourning and we shall resume at 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before giving the floor to the Prosecution to open this hearing which is taking place in connection with Rule 61, the Chamber would like to make known a decision bearing on inviting amicus curiae during the proceedings. I would now like to read this decision to you. The Trial Chamber I of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, considering that pursuant to Rule 74 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Trial Chamber may, if it considers it desirable in the interests of the proper administration of justice, invite or grant leave to any State, organisation or individual to make a presentation on any issue it deems relevant; that this rule appears in Chapter 6 on Proceedings before Trial Chambers. Considering, however, that the requirement of the proper administration of justice is a principle which must prevail during all phases of the legal proceedings before an international criminal tribunal and not only during the trial itself. Considering that, in addition, to must be mentioned that, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 89(A), the Rules of evidence are applicable to all proceedings before the Trial Chambers, including the proceedings conducted in accordance with Rule 61. Considering, furthermore, that recourse to the amicus curiae, an impartial personality, only for the purposes of making a statement on an issue which the Trial Chamber considers relevant and dealing with the presentation of information and not evidence, appears fully legitimate and entirely consistent with the proper administration of justice. Considering in this case, that during the hearings in respect of the Prosecution against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic pursuant to the provisions of Rule 61, the Trial Chamber considers it desirable to hear the explanations and information of two amicus curiaes concerning the status of human rights and the campaign of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1992 and the disappearances following the events at Srebrenica on the one hand, and, on the other, the practice of rape and sexual assault as part of the ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1992. Considering that each of the amicus curiae, if he considers it relevant to support his presentation, may submit any documents, reports or partial reports. Considering, therefore that, for these purposes, the Trial Chamber is inviting two personalities it deems competent. For the forgoing reasons, pursuant to Rule 74 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, invites Mrs. Elizabeth Rehn, Special Rapporteur of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights to appear on 5th July 1996 as an amicus curiae as part of the hearings on proceedings initiated against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 61, so that she may make a presentation on the status of human rights and the campaign of ethnic cleansing of Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1992 as well as on the disappearances following the events at Srebrenica. Invites Mrs. Christine Cleiren, a member of the Commission of Experts established pursuant to Security Council resolution 780 (1992) to appear on 1 July 1996 as an amicus curiae as part of the hearings on proceedings initiated against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 61, so that she may make a presentation on the practice of rape and sexual assault as part of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1992 and on the conclusions of that Commission on those issues. States that the amicus curiae may submit to the Trial Chamber any documents, reports, or partial reports that they deem relevant. Dated this 26th day of June 1996, International Criminal Tribunal at the Hague, the Netherlands. I would now like to ask the prosecuting counsel to take the floor to open our Rule 61 hearing concerning the two accused, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Now, at last, we submit to you for your determination under Rule 61 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence the two indictments in respect of the two Bosnian-Serb leaders, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, that have just been read out in open court. Due to the reading by the Registrar in toto of the indictments through which the accused have been thoroughly introduced and all the charges against them brought forward in public, I can drastically shorten my opening statement and then do it more or less extemporarily. As appears from the crimes charged in the two indictments against the accused, Karadzic and Mladic, they encompass the commission of the whole range of serious violation of humanitarian law in the material competence of this Tribunal, committed under a protracted time on a huge scale in a widespread and systematic way leading to the loss of thousands and again thousands of civilian lives. A detailed account of the magnitude and the horrors of the crimes has through the reading of the indictments already been brought to your Honour and to the public. What, however, we will hear today and during the following six days, will not cover all of the evidence we have available for trial because a 61 hearing in itself is limited in scope. In setting the scene for the evidence we are going to bring before the Trial Chamber, I will now restrict myself to a few important facts, give examples, summarise what we are going to bring before you and address some legal issues. First, as to our evidence that we will start to bring today, I will give you a short overview so you know what we are going to put forward. After my opening statement, we will call Professor Paul Garde to give a general historical overview of the involvements of the events in Bosnia and the rest of the former Yugoslavia, to put the picture, the context, in which we put all our evidence. Then we will ask one of our investigators, Mr. John Ralston, to give a brief summary of the evidence collected to show what happened as a background to the first of the two indictments. To that indictment, as far as it concerns the shelling of Sarajevo, we will bring one or another of one of our investigators, Mr. Jan Van Hecke, who will tell us about the siege and sniping of the city of Sarajevo. To that effect, we will also bring the Mayor of Sarajevo who, we suggest, will paint a picture from the inside of the besieged city during this long time that that city was besieged. We have then a portion with relation to rapes and sexual assaults where one of our investigators will bring a brief relation of what this investigation has brought to light. A person by the name of Colin Kaizer is a specialist of sacred and historical monuments and the destruction which took place in Bosnia against places of historic and religious importance. A Canadian soldier taken hostage will tell about his experience being treated like that in his service as a UN soldier. Our investigator, Jean Rene Ruiz, will tell us about what happened as an overview of what happened in connection with the fall of the safe area of Srebrenica. I will come back to what we will do with people from the Dutch battalion. A victim, who I do not want to name now, from the events in Srebrenica after the fall of the city will also tell his own experiences. We will bring multiple witnesses covering the events in Srebrenica as a whole. I will now just point to some of these things we have already heard and to stress some facts. As you heard, the detainees were repeatedly subjected to inhumane acts, including murder, rape, sexual assault, torture, beatings, robbery as well as other forms of mental and physical abuse. In many instances, you will remember on the reading of the indictments, women and girls who were detained were raped in the camps where they were kept and also taken out of these camps and brought to other places or localities and being there also raped or otherwise sexually abused. Another way of destroying the ethnicity of the Muslim and Croatian populations was the targeting of political leaders. As you heard, intellectuals, professional men and women were arrested, physically abused and many times murdered in towns and villages which happened in Prijedor, Vlasenica and Bosanski Samac. A third way of committing crimes against humanity was deportation. Thousands of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the areas of Prijedor, Vlasenica, Bosanski Samac, Brcko and Foca, among others, were systematically arrested and interned in detention facilities established all around Bosnia under the supervision of the Serb military under the ultimate command of the two indictees. Yet another criminal method used to inflict conditions of life calculated to bring about a destruction of those groups were the shelling of civilian gatherings and their appropriation, plunder and extensive destruction as set out in the indictment which has been read out to you. I will also point out and remind you concerning the sniping and shelling of Sarajevo and the indictment, therefore, lists of children, civilians, women and men killed or wounded in this sniping campaign brought about by the accused Karadzic and Mladic and charged as the crime against humanity, as you heard incorporated in our indictment. The first indictment deals finally with the taking of hostages of United Nations peace-keepers. I would like to stress that some of these hostage taken people, including Canadian, Czech, Russian, Nigerian, Pakistani and Swedish officers, were immediately selected for use as human shields to prevent air strikes by NATO at ammunition bunkers and communication centres. These acts are, as you heard, charged as grave breaches and violations of customs of war. As to what happened after the fall of Srebrenica, your Honours, you will be told how the column in the woods was ambushed and attacked with artillery shells, anti-aircraft guns, automatic weapons and the like. You will hear estimations of how many of the thousands fleeing people lost their lives in an attempt to reach safety, being fired at, executed or committing suicide under the tremendous pressure. Thousands, as you heard, of these Muslims in the column, however, surrendered to the Bosnian military having been assured that they would not be harmed. Some of the soldiers giving such assurances were, as you heard, wearing UN uniforms and blue helmets. The captive men were taken to large assembly points near Karkaj, where the accused Mladic was present. You will hear summaries of witnesses' statements stating that thousands of men who had surrendered were summarily executed at Karkaj and other places by the forces under the command of Ratko Mladic. As mentioned, a Dutch battalion was stationed in a compound in Potocari to which thousands of refugees went for shelter. You will hear Colonel Karremans, Chief of the Dutch Battalion, and two other Dutch military men, all of them present and on duty in Potocari these days in July 1995, telling you about their efforts to shelter the refugees, and what happened to these refugees and of their meetings with Ratko Mladic and of the statements and actions of Ratko Mladic. These witnesses and others will tell you about summary executions around the compound in Potocari, and of men transported to Karkaj and then massacred by Bosnian Serb military personnel. In summary, your Honours, the attack on the United Nations safe area of Srebrenica and the actions by Bosnian Serb forces that followed under the command of Ratko Mladic, and with the consent from the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, resulted in the virtual destruction of the Muslim population -- 60,000 people -- of that area. I do not hesitate to add Srebrenica to the list of names such as Katyn, Lidice, Oradour and Kragujevac and to pronounce it the most horrendous, unimaginable war crime committed in Europe since the end of World War II. It was a crime committed and directed at an area under peaceful United Nations protection in obvious and complete contempt and defiance of the international community, the Security Council and humanitarian law -- and of this Tribunal. One of the principal objectives of our Tribunal is to act as a powerful deterrent to all parties against continued participation in inhumane acts. It is discouraging and frustrating to note that in this case the existence of the Tribunal, apparently, did not have any impact. It is even more frustrating to note that the States and other actors on the international scene, on whose co-operation we depend and who have the power and the tools to act, have not executed the warrants of this Tribunal. Let it be known that what the Prosecution really wants to do is to try the accuseds for the crimes alleged against them here, in this courtroom, in The Hague, not just having this 61 rule hearing. However, in the course of satisfying the Trial Chamber that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused committed the crimes charged in the indictments, I will now turn to some legal issues. It is the submission of the Prosecution that at all times relevant to this indictment an international armed conflict existed between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the one hand, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on the other hand, and that the Serb administration in Pale is in this context to be considered an agent of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. To substantiate that, we have submitted to the Trial Chamber a brief on the application of Article 2 of the Statute and the existence of an international armed conflict for this hearing. The key argument in this brief is that this conflict can be classified as international on the basis of the direct military involvement of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its successor, the Federal Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on the existence of hostilities and the partial occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was the result. The brief is supported by material which demonstrates that reasonable grounds exist for believing that the parties were directly involved in an armed conflict and that Bosnia and Herzegovina was partly occupied. I will finally touch on two other legal issues pertaining to the indictments, namely, the crime of genocide and the doctrine of superior authority. Genocide is the ultimate crime. It is characterised by the particular intent, or dolus specialis, to destroy a group "as such". It is this fundamental element which distinguishes genocide from the ordinary crime of murder. In the words of the Israeli District Court in the Eichmann case, I quote, "the special character" of genocide is the "general and total" intent to physically exterminate members of a group "as such". The term "in whole or in part" in article 4 of our Statute clearly indicates that the intent to destroy does not have to be directed against the entire group. The term "in part" is ambiguous and lends itself to differing interpretations. However, it is the submission of the Prosecution that it implies, to quote the official report of a UN expert on genocide, "a reasonably significant number, relative to the total of the group as a whole, or else a significance section of a group such as its leadership". This is taken from the Whitaker report at page 16, paragraph 29. In view of the particular intent requirement, which is the essence of the crime of genocide, the relative proportionate scale of the actual or attempted physical destruction of a group, or a significant section thereof, should be considered in relation to the factual opportunity of the accused to destroy a group in a specific geographical area within the sphere of his control, and not in relation to the entire population of the group in a wider geographical sense. In all cases, it is the submission of the Prosecution that in the interests of international justice, genocide should not be diluted or belittled by too broad an interpretation. Indeed, it should be reserved only for acts of exceptional gravity and magnitude which shock the conscience of humankind and which, therefore, justify the appellation of genocide as the "ultimate crime". The accused Karadzic and Mladic are charged, inter alia, with participation in crimes against humanity and genocide; crimes which are inherently massive and systematic and which, therefore, almost without exception, require a common plan or design formulated and organised at the highest level of authority. Indeed, it is the Prosecutor's case that without their instigation and plans for the creation of "ethnically pure" regions, or at least without their acquiescence, ordinary Yugoslav citizens would not have had the means or the resources to commit atrocities on such a vast scale. Therefore, it would be justified to say that the higher up the chain of command that we go, the higher the degree of responsibility for the atrocities which were ultimately executed by the common soldier on the ground. The doctrine of superior responsibility applies to any person in a line of command who has a personal responsibility with regard to the perpetrator of the acts concerned because the latter, being his subordinate, is under his control; in the present case, it is alleged that this would clearly apply to the accused Karadzic and Mladic with respect to all members of the Bosnian-Serb Army as well as other armed groups and units including the Police Force. The Prosecution wishes to point out that in the case of the commanders with executive authority over a territory which is occupied or otherwise under their de facto control, meaning in this case the Pale administration or the so-called "Republika Srpska" during the period covered by the indictment, responsibility extends to "maintaining peace and order, punishing crime and protecting lives and property". To quote the decision of the US Military Tribunal in the Hostages Trial of 1947, the responsibility of such a commander "is general and not limited to a control of units directly under his command". I have taken this out of the law reports of the trial of war criminals, volume 8, page 71. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the widespread and systematic nature of "ethnic cleansing" and other massive atrocities against the non-Serb civilian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, allegedly committed by the direct subordinates of the accused as well as other persons under their control, can lead to no other conclusion than the allegation that the accused ordered their commission, or at least, acquiesced in their commission through failing to prevent or punish such criminal acts. The Prosecution submits that it would be inconceivable to suggest that the accused Karadzic and Mladic had not given their approval to the massive criminal policy of "ethnic cleansing", often genocidal in character, which was committed by their subordinates, and which lasted for some three and a half years. Accordingly, under Article 7, paragraph 3, of the Statute, they have been charged with individual criminal responsibility for the actions of their subordinates, amounting to war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. To finish, your Honours, the scope of a Rule 61 hearing is not only for the Prosecutor to satisfy the Trial Chamber that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused have committed the crimes charged in the indictments, and for the Chamber, if satisfied, to so determine and to issue arrest warrants to be transmitted to all States. It is also (and most importantly so) to assess the question whether the Prosecutor has satisfied the Trial Chamber that the failure to effect personal service was due in whole or in part to a failure or refusal of a State to co-operate with the Tribunal in accordance with Article 29 of our Statute. In the case of the accused Karadzic and Mladic, it is the submission of the Prosecution that the failure to arrest them and surrender them to the Tribunal is blatant refusal by the State of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to co-operate with this Tribunal. During the course of this hearing, I will tender evidence showing that that State has had multiple opportunities to arrest the accused but, contrary to its obligation, has not done so. The Bosnian Serb administration in Pale, or Republika Srpska, if you like, a self-proclaimed entity de facto exercising governmental functions and thus, by the definitions of our Rules, a State, has also refused to co-operate with the Tribunal in accordance with the Statute by ignoring its warrants. It is, therefore, the request of the Prosecution that, in addition to the issuance of international arrest warrants, this Chamber should also certify to the President of the Tribunal that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale have failed to comply with their obligations under Article 29 of the Statute, and further recommend to the President that he notify the Security Council of this refusal. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, thank you. I would like to put to you a question. Yes, I have a question for you. Thank you, Prosecutor. My first question put by the Tribunal is a matter of organisation. Do you intend to submit a document concerning the schedule of testimonies to the members of this court, a schedule or a timetable such as you read out at the beginning of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Our answer, your Honour, is no. We are not absolutely certain when, how many and who will come. So, we have this outline schedule, I think, already in your possession.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We cannot present something precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Right, thank you, Prosecutor. I have a second question. I thought I understood that you would ask for protective measures for some of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Some of them have not definitely taken any standpoint to the question of the need of protection. Until we know for certain, we will not alert the protection unit, but we will have them informed exactly what is happening.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Thank you, Prosecutor. So without further delay could we possibly usher in the first witness, Mr. Mark Harmon or ---

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Mr. Bowers.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Bowers. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right, I am looking at the clock. I suppose that, yes, we resumed at 4 o'clock, I guess. Just to give you some idea as to the duration of your examination, I suggest that we take a short break at around half past 5. Then we will resume today at around quarter to 6 until 7 o'clock today -- just for you to get organised on the basis of this timetable which is rather exceptional and will apply for today only. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: That sounds fine, your Honour. The Prosecutor, your Honours, would call Professor Paul Garde to the stand, please. ^^ PROFESSOR PAUL GARDE, called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps while we are waiting we have three binders with exhibits that we can present to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor, please be seated. You are going to be given your headphones. Would you please rise and take your oath. Usher, would you please hand out the declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, all the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Professor. First, can you tell me if you can hear me? Can you hear the Prosecutor? Can you hear the interpreter? Please let us know anyway. Professor, you appear here as a witness called by the Prosecution and you appear before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Prosecutor, you now have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Initially, we have separate binders for the court and we would like to present those to the usher for presentation to the Judges. These will contain all the exhibits that Professor Garde will refer to during his testimony. For the sake of efficiency, we will not be tendering any of these exhibits until the end of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Professor Garde, would you please begin by stating your full name and spelling it for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Paul Garde, Paul, P-A-U-L, Garde, G-A-R-D-E.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Professor, would you please tell the court briefly about academic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am a specialist in Slav linguistics. I am a Professor in grammar in Russian I taught. I was a Professor of Slav literature and languages at the University in Aix-en-Provence since 64 until 89 when I retired. I also taught as a guest teacher in the States, at the Yale -- at Columbia University and in Switzerland at the University of Geneva. I have published about 10 books concerning Slav linguistics and, more recently, on issues concerning the former Yugoslavia and I have also published about 150 articles on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit 1 that we have provided the court contains a listing of the Professor's various writings for reference. Professor Garde, would you tell the court when and how you first developed an academic interest in the region of the former Yugoslavia, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is difficult to differentiate the academic interest from my own interest. I started visiting Yugoslavia back in 51 as a specialist in Slav languages. Yugoslavia at the time was the only Slav country that I could easily have access to. This is why from that early date I kept returning to that country. Might I add that I visited all the Yugoslav republics practically every single year for the past 40 years. Of course, I took a special interest in Yugoslavia from an academic point of view. As a specialist in Slav languages, I of course dealt with, compared Slav languages and 1,000 Slav languages, and I wrote a certain number of articles concerning those languages. I have also participated in numerous conferences, seminars, and at different republics of the former Yugoslavia. I was in contact with the linguists from these republics. I also attended debates on languages that took place at the time. More specifically, since '91, since the outbreak of the war, so far my interest had focused exclusively or essentially on linguistic problems, but since the war started, since I wanted to look at the historical and political problems of that country, I turned more to that sort of issues in the past five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Professor Garde, what are the languages spoken in the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia different languages are spoken. First, the language that was called for a long time Serbo-Croat, now we call it, or we distinguish between Serb, Croat and Bosnian; then you have Slovene, Macedonian, which are also Slav languages and, of course, many other languages are spoken, more specifically, Albanian, Hungarian, which are not Slav languages and which are spoken by different minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Professor, are you fluent in any of these languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I fluently speak and write Serbo-Croat in its different forms and I read and I understand without any difficulty Macedonian, and I have a bit more difficulty understanding Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: I assume you also have a working knowledge of the two alphabets used in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. Yes, of course -- no problems with the alphabets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you just briefly describe for the court the two alphabets and the regions in which they are used, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Cyrillic alphabet is used in Serbia and Macedonia; the Latin alphabet is used in Slovenia -- sorry, in Serbia, Slovenia and Montenegro, and the Latin alphabet is used in Croatia, in Slovenia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina both alphabets are used with the predominance of the Latin alphabet today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Did you write a fairly major book concerning the breakup and dissolution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote a book titled "Life and Death of Yugoslavia". This was published in Paris, Fayard publishing house in '92, in which I briefly presented a summary of the different countries that made up the former Yugoslavia. Then I described these different countries and, finally, I analysed the crisis which was the source of the outbreak of Yugoslavia starting in '86 until the date of the end of my book which was '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was there something that caused you to write this book or prompted you to begin this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I started writing this book in July '91 and I finished it in March '92. So what prompted me to write this book is more specifically at the time when the war started, it started from a military point of view in June '91. Well, right afterwards I realised to what extent in France, at least, the public opinion, the media, and even all leaders were totally ignorant of what was taking place in this country. I was appalled to hear what was being said, what was being written, at the time. So, all of a sudden I realised that the experience of that country that I had grown familiar with in the past 40 years, and I naively thought that everybody shared the same experience, so I realised all of a sudden that my experience could probably benefit something to the public, that I could probably correct some mistakes of judgments, some misunderstandings, by putting forth all the different facts. I thought it was, sort of, like a duty on my part to inform the public, and this is why I started writing this book which I completed in a couple of months or in a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Professor Garde, what type of research did you do in connection with writing this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to write this book, on the one hand, I collected material, I read everything I could possibly find on the history of that country and, furthermore, also carried out some interviews with people from the former Republics of Yugoslavia that lived in France. I also reviewed all the press. I read a great number of magazines, of papers, coming from the different Yugoslav republics from the year 1991/92, and that review of the press coming from the various republics of Yugoslavia contributed a lot of material which made it possible to write this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that for the past five years, at least, you have been devoting most of your efforts to studying, writing and lecturing on the changing situations in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is absolutely right. For the past five years I have practically done nothing else but to try to collect material on this issue, of course, while I was writing the book, but also in the following years I have continued collecting material, I have continued reading, reviewing the press, talking with people, travelling over there and I have tried to convey my findings to the public through writing articles, lecturing and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Have you had an occasion to advise the French government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened to me but only on an occasional basis. I was asked twice to produce reports for CAP, which is the centre of forecast and analysis of the French Foreign Ministry. I submitted my report in January '93 on Serb nationalism. In September of the same year, I produced a same report on the Croat nationalism. Then I was also invited for consultation by various Ministers, once in December '92 by George Kiejman who at the time was Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs in the Beregovoy government, and later on in the spring of '95 I was invited by Francois Leotard, then Defence Minister in the Balladur government. I also was invited by President Chirac but in the company of 10 other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Professor Garde, what did you do in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To prepare my testimony of today, I came twice to The Hague. I had interviews with the representative of the Prosecution, and I looked at the various materials that were handed out to me by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At this point, for the court's benefit and our benefit, would you begin your substantive testimony with just a brief historical review of some of the key events in the geographical region that is known as the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the former Yugoslavia, in the western part of the Balkans, you have different peoples living there that speak the same language or similar languages, the southern Slavic languages, and you have peoples who for a long time have belonged to different cultural areas. You have the Serbs and Macedonians that belonged to western Christianity or orthodoxy, then you have the Croats that belong to western Christianity, to Catholicism. So, basically, you have different cultural backgrounds and you have sociological different habits, as it were. Back in the Middle Ages at different times you had Serb states, you had Croat states, you had Bosnian states, at different times, and on different areas, covering different areas, and in modern times, as applied to the rest of the Balkans, you had the Ottoman Empire and the regions in the north west were excluded from the Ottoman Empire and belonged to the Habsburg Empire. The Ottoman Empire and the Turk conquest meant that you had a third religion that came into play and a third type of sociological background, which is Islam and which a large portion of the inhabitants of Bosnia converted to Islam. The ancestors of the present Muslims and the people from the Albania converted to Islam, so that is a third religion. This meant that there were major migrations, moves of populations, which explained the mix up of populations today. All these different peoples back in the 19th century have realised that they belonged to a nation. This is the time of nationalism, of this nation awareness, of what is called national "renaissance". These peoples tried to get their independence and those that were under the Ottoman Empire wanted to become independent through armed actions, rights. This was the case of Serbia which was the first to organise a sort of uprising. The State got organised at the beginning of the 19th century in the former Austrian part. On the contrary, this national awakening was more based on cultural and political, because they had a political struggle within the Habsburg Empire, and at the time you had the different ways of thinking in terms of the future of these countries. You had also had national movements, and the first one was the Serb national movement. In the constitution of Greater Serbia, that was a State that would gather all Serbs. You also had a Croat national tendency in other regions as well. At the same time you had another trend that surfaced amongst the southern Serbs that were under Austrian authority which is called the Yugoslav Movement. The Yugoslav Movement meant the idea that since all these peoples are neighbours and speak about the same language, the southern Slavic languages, why could they not in one way or another get together? One of the main samples or spokesmen of this idea was a Bishop Josip Strossmayer. All these movements grew or developed in parallel in the course of the 19th century. In 1918, at the end of the First World War, a State was created, a common State, which later was called Yugoslavia. But that State was founded on a misunderstanding right from the start, because in the eyes of the Serbs, who were the founding fathers of that State, the Serbs who had won the First World War along with the allies, but at the cost of enormous sacrifices, so for them the State was sort of the crowning of their victory, but for them that State was the realisation of their product of a Greater Serbia. The main advantage is that all Serbs would belong to one single State. For the other peoples, on the contrary, the main advantage of that State was understood as reuniting together on an equal footing several different peoples. That misunderstanding or this different interpretation has never stopped influencing the development of events and, undoubtedly, it still plays a role to explain the present events. These two interpretations, the first one being that the state of Yugoslavia as being understood as the realisation of the Greater Serbia project is the interpretation of the Yugoslav monarchy between 1918 and 1941. That monarchy, the king was Serb, the political leaders were Serb and the Serbs considered it as a continuation of their State, and the other peoples considered it as an oppressive force. Now, the second interpretation, i.e. Yugoslavia as reuniting several peoples on equal footings, was essentially the interpretation of the second Yugoslavia, that of Tito, between '49 and '91. In between, between the two, you had of course the Second World Ward. The Second World War which is, of course, a very dark period, a time of horror where we saw the immediate defeat and the breaking up of Yugoslavia with collaborating fascist State established on the territory of Croatia; a time when we saw a collaborating government in the territory of Serbia with terrible massacres and genocide of Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia by the fascist Ustasha state in Croatia; but at the same time we had Muslim massacres and Croat massacres by Serb Chetniks. We also saw another resistance movement outside the Chetnik set of the partisans, the communist partisans, under the leadership of Tito who officially was a pluri-ethnic, was supposed to gather all the peoples, and this is possibly the main reason for his victory. So, but, of course, naturally, this time of horrors has left an impact in the later period, and so it is remembering, the fact that they remember these terrible massacres, these reciprocal massacres, and this still has an influence today. The Tito regime was first founded in principle on a refusal or a rejection of what had been the principal state of the preceding monarchy, that is, a rejection of the domination by one people over the others. As a result, the Yugoslavia under Tito was officially created as a federation, a federation of several republics which were autonomous, each one representing and corresponding more or less perfectly, but in fact imperfectly, to the different peoples constituting them; and that Tito Yugoslavia was founded on the federal principle, therefore, on decentralisation with the autonomy of the various provinces and republics, and the autonomy became increasingly real as the regime became entrenched. For example, the constitution of 1974 granted much more extensive jurisdiction and competence of regions of each of the provinces and republics, so that one was moving in that constitution of 1974, moving toward an almost confederate system, but at the same time it was not a truly autonomy of the various peoples because the regime was after all a communist one, a dictatorial regime, even though it was much less stringent than that of the other communist countries all around it. Therefore, despite everything, the regime controlled the power, and the autonomy that was given to the various provinces and to the republics was really, in fact, the autonomy of the leaders in each of those republics rather than the peoples, although democracy, of course, did play a certain role in the events which were to follow. Whatever the case, this movement toward a greater degree of decentralisation to greater autonomy among the provinces and the republics was, of course, interpreted differently by the different peoples; because each new step taken towards decentralization was welcomed by the different peoples, except the Serbs who wished a greater centralised position and were not particularly pleased with the increasing decentralisation because the Serbs found themselves distributed among several of the provinces of the republics, that is all except one, and wanted there to be greater connections between these different provinces. They wanted a centralised state and that the other people, on the other hand, wanted a very stronger decentralised state. All of these conflicting elements burst out later on during the 1980s once Tito had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Garde. Your Honours, given the limited time and scope of this particular hearing, we have obviously presented a very condensed view of the initial historical background of this particular conflict, but we would pause at this point; if there are any specific questions that the court would like to ask Professor Garde with regard to the general historical back drop that he has just presented to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will consult with my colleagues, Mr. Bowers. We did not have to speak very long, but we just wonder whether it might be better to ask questions at the very end of Professor Garde's presentation or whether there might be another way of organising the testimony to ask questions. I think that, in fact, we will ask a few questions. I think Judge Riad has a few questions he wants to ask. Would you like to ask your question now, Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor Garde, my question may anticipate a bit what you are going to say later on, but since you have already spoken about the idea of Greater Serbia, I would be very interested in knowing how this idea developed through the current conflict and who were those who were the champions of that idea and what was the origin Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 42 to 72. of it, because apparently during Tito's days the idea had disappeared during that second phase, which you said was rather one of coexistence among the various communities. So, how was this idea able to come about again and to whom do we owe, or to what do we owe, this renaissance? Who were those who encouraged it and who carried it out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One cannot say that this is an idea that disappeared. This is an idea which had been very powerful during the 19th century and during the first half of the 20th century. The idea was under Tito's authority something which was not allowed, one was not to express it, but it expressed itself, nonetheless, in the Serbian press outside the country. For example, in the United States or in Australia and other countries as well, where there were Serbian newspapers which expressed very openly that idea. The Serbs, in fact, were not the only ones; there were also an overseas Croatian press which expressed nationalistic thoughts as well. So the idea was partially kept by those who were no longer living in the country and also present all the time in Serbia itself, even though it was not expressed, at least in the beginning, and in any case, under the Tito regime, since it was understood that the nationalist tendencies in the various republics continued to exist, the government in principle condemned them, officially condemned them, in the name of a doctrine known as unity and fraternity. But, simultaneously, they had a role to play and used them because the regime played with the different nationalist aspirations, pitting one against the other. It would in certain regions favour one people at the expense of another. Direct expression of these aspirations under the most brutal forms was smothered, but the indirect expression of those ideas through literature or through various concrete demands sometimes could appear. During the first half of the government's existence, the Ministry of the Interior was the person who was the most powerful in the police was himself a Serb -- this was the period when the regime was extremely centralised -- and this is the person who became actually the person who was involved, who repressed the Albanians and advocated that repression. We can, therefore, see that these nationalistic tendencies always existed, and that at one point they were expressed more openly. For example, at the end of the 1970s with Dobrica Cosic who later on in 1992 was the President of the new Yugoslavia who had, in fact, expressed various theses which earned him being removed from power or being removed from the good graces of the government. But, in principle, at that point it was not -- so long as the Yugoslav Federation was still in existence, it was not a question of demands for modifying or changing the borders of Yugoslavia, because they were borders which were satisfactory to the Serbs, but had to do, rather, with demands for this or that point, having to do with relations among the different nations within each of the republics. These trends became more clear once Tito had died, that is, during the 1980s which is when they began to be manifest; for example, having to do with the events of Kosovo where there was a conflict between the Serbs and the Albanians when even the official press condemned the position of the Albanians and took the position which was very much in favour of the Serbs. The same thing held in literature at that time when we see appearing or, at least, begin seeing again people who are presenting things from the point of view of Serbian nationalism, for example, with the novel which was written by Vuk Draskovic called "The Knife", which appeared in 1982 and I remember that very well. So the nationalist Serbian tendencies became more and more strong during that time, but so long as the Federal State existed, the problem did not really arise as having to do with the creation of Serbia because the Federal State, so long as its practices and constitution was directed in a certain sense, the government could, in fact, become the realisation itself of Greater Serbia. Therefore, the very term "Greater Serbia" really is not correctly used for that period, and the concept of the Greater Serbia did not have to be used and should not be used. But these nationalist Serbian tendencies became more and more clear throughout the 1980s and become particularly distinct in the memorandum of the Academy of Sciences which was drafted at the end of 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When we talk about politics and the leadership, can this concept be attributed to a certain faction or to specific individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can attribute it to a whole range of people. It was a project which was floating in the air at the time all through the 1980s, that this idea of reforming Yugoslavia in order to turn it into something, to be more of a centralised state, the idea which we find in this memorandum of the Academy of Sciences which I have just mentioned is the following: This attempt at decentralisation first led to economic disaster and then meant that the Serbs were divided among various more ever increasing autonomous entities, and that they felt that they had been oppressed and that they had to arise by creating a centralised state. So the idea was already floating in the air. It was promoted by various politicians, by people working in universities, those who wanted to become the leaders of the political parties later on, that is, people like Draskovic, who later on would found the Serbian Renewal Movement, or Seselj, who later would set up the Radical Party, those who would later on set up the Democratic Party; that is, it was also propagated more insidiously by the official press. The great event, the great change, takes place in 1986/86 when all of a sudden these ideas, which to this point had more or less been fought by the regime who considered them as really being dangerous, suddenly there was a communist leader in Serbia, a new leader, who adopted them. This was Milan Milosevic who came to power in 1986 and affirmed his power once again in '87. From that point on, these ideas, which up to that point had been propagated more or less by various people, suddenly were taken up again by the power, the power of Serbia. They were no longer considered, whereas up to this point they had been fought against, but from this point on, on the contrary, they were encouraged at the highest places. This is how things happened more or less. I am not sure that I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes. You answered them very, very well. But did these ideas correspond to any kind of a concrete reality on the ground having to do with the way the communities were distributed, but was this kind of instead an expansionist idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So long as Yugoslavia existed as a Federal State, the purpose of the Serbian nationalists was merely to strengthen the State, to reinforce the centralisation within that State, to reinforce the federal power against the various entities, because the federal power conceived in that way could become the instrument of Serb domination on the rest. At that point, there were no territorial demands. There was no reason to have any because it would have been sufficient for the power at the federal level to become once again stronger and more centralising for the objectives of the Serb nationalists to be achieved. It was only gradually, in fact, that this ideal moved away and that, on the other hand, the central power became less central and that the provinces acquired more autonomy. At that point, the idea begins to be born, that perhaps it would be better to come to an accommodation with the fact that there are borders between the republics and, therefore, attempt to shift the borders, at which point the idea begins to come about that a redistribution of the territory would become necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Perhaps there are some other questions, Mr. Bowers, but, of course, since we do not know all the things that you are going to say or the structure of what you have prepared or what Mr. Garde has prepared, myself along with my colleagues would prefer that you continue as you are going and, if necessary, we might go back to ask some questions, but for the time being we think it might be best for you continue. I give the floor back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: I want to give the court some opportunity, if there were some pressing questions that were generated from the initial overview. Professor Garde, after World War II, the country became the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would like to have Exhibit 2 displayed -- it is R1-5 -- and is a map of the Federative Yugoslavia. This would be Exhibit 2 in your binders. We have it on the computer screen now. Professor Garde, would you just use the map and describe the basic political structure of the Federative Republic between the end of World War II and the death of Tito, pointing out the different political components that are shown on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia was composed of six republics, that is, in the north west there was Slovenia, then Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Macedonia and Serbia. The Republic of Serbia, which is the largest with the largest population, within it had two autonomous provinces, that is, in the north it was Vojvodina and in the south was Kosovo. The raison d'etre for this division along borders, which in most cases represented the historic borders and where there was a presence of various types of people, of which the constitution officially recognised since the beginning that there were five people of the southern Slavs, and then later on after '68 there was a sixth which was the Bosnian, the Muslim Bosnians and, therefore, there were six peoples for which six republics corresponded. There were the Croats, the Slovenes, the Muslim Bosnians, the Montenegrins, the Macedonians and the Serbs. However, since we are talking about historic borders which did not correspond to the ethnic borders -- in fact, there really were no ethnic borders because it was impossible to draw the lines according to ethnic lines; they were such a mixture of peoples -- in some of the republics one noted that there was a presence not of one but several people making it up. Therefore, in Macedonian, Serbia was supposed to have only one nation making it up, one people making it up, Croatia had two, that is, the Croats and the Serbs, since there were 12 per cent Serb population, according to the 1991 population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where there were three peoples, that is, the Muslim Bosnians, the Serbs and the Croats who in 1991 were 44 per cent, 31 per cent and 18 per cent. In addition, outside those people who made up the southern Slavs, there were other populations as well that were called either the minorities or nationalities. In any case, these were peoples who lived in the territory of Yugoslavia but who were not part of the southern Slavs and most of whom corresponded to a state which existed out of Yugoslavia. The two major minorities were the Albanians, represented by 2 million and the Hungarians either 300,000 or 400,000. This is why, as far as Serbia was concerned, there were two autonomous provinces created; in the southern part, Kosovo, because the population there was a majority Albanian, and then in Vojvodina because next to the Serbian population, which in 1991 represented 54 per cent, I believe, there were several other, a large number of minorities, in fact, mostly Hungarians who were the largest, but there were Rumanians, there were Slovaks. That is two regions where minorities that were very significant existed. One of the peculiarities of the constitution under Tito of the various constitutions which followed one after the another during the regime was the fact that while they proclaimed that there was equality among the various nationalities, it maintained the distinction between the peoples, on the one hand, and the nationalities and minorities on the other. There was a kind of hierarchy and at the same time this hierarchy between the republics which corresponded to the peoples and the autonomous provinces which corresponded to the minorities. The status of the autonomous provinces, well, I believe that this hierarchy was maintained despite the theoretical principle of equality. This was one of the difficulties of the regime and which was reflected also in the existence of a disparity between the idea of autonomous provinces and republics. There was a constitutional contradiction in the 1974 constitution. At the same time it was stated that Kosovo and Vojvodina were part of the Republic of Serbia, but simultaneously it is said, well, one reads, that Kosovo and Vojvodina had the same, just as the other ones are parts of the Republic. So this puts everything together and separates everything which corresponds to the difficulty and to the conflict which existed between the Serbs, on the one hand, and the minorities who were living in Serbian territory on the other and then between the Serbs and the Albanians. So this is what the structure was and within the structure, as the regime evolved, the republics became more and more autonomous, but the autonomous provinces also became increasingly autonomous. From '74, they were on the same footing as the republics, which was a source of a great deal of dissatisfaction among the Serbs. I would like to add as well that when I said that the republics corresponded to this or that, people, does that mean that any of these republics were really homogeneous, because all of the provinces, all of the republics, had a mixed population of different proportions. I will not give you the details here, but the ethnic composition of each of the regions was extremely complex.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Before you arrived, we had provided for a recess so that you could catch your breathe. Now would be an appropriate time, it is 5.30, and we shall resume in 15 minutes at quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting counsel, we have given a bad example here. We have taken a little longer, we, Judges, but we will try to catch up on that in our further discussions, so you have the floor. We are looking forward to hearing more from Professor Garde.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Professor Garde, when we just before the break you had mentioned ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The microphone, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Professor Garde, before the break you had been discussing the concept of peoples as a nation under the Yugoslav concept. I think it would be helpful if you could just describe for the court the significance of this nation status as a people for the citizens of Yugoslavia and how they viewed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that part of Europe the state emerged after the nation in western Europe, the modern state is of an old phenomenon, as it were, and the nation emerged subsequently. For example, come the 18th century with the French Revolution, people belonging to a same state realised that they were part of a community which is the nation. So, belonging to a nation, for example, be it French or British, is the same thing as belonging to the state. So it is one and the same thing, belonging to the state or belonging to the nation. But in central and eastern Europe, on the other hand, the nation, the concept of nation, appeared also after the French Revolution in the 18th century and these nations did not have a state. "Nation" is considered to be a group of people sharing a common culture, a number of cultural characteristics, and these cultural characteristics are something that remain with them regardless of the state they belong to.
